stories.headline: Netanyahu govt rejects flydubai bid to resume Israel flights after cockpit attack
stories.bodyText:
Benjamin Netanyahu-led Israel has declined flydubai's request to resume its flight operations to the country, a week after an Omani co-pilot attacked Captain Smit Machchar midair on a Tel Aviv-bound flight. The attack put the lives of more than 170 people at risk.
Flydubai had sought permission to resume its Israel operations, saying an investigation into the incident was nearing completion and that several employees had been fired, Israel-based Channel 13 reported.
The incident involved Indian captain Smit Machchar and Omani co-pilot Hammam al-Hammami, who attacked the captain in the cockpit.
Most of the more than 170 passengers on board were Israeli citizens.
According to the report, officials from Israel’s transportation ministry have also been invited to visit Dubai next week.
However, transportation minister Miri Regev has declined the airline’s request for now, the report said.
Meanwhile, details of the injuries suffered by Machchar during the incident have emerged, highlighting the severity of the attack he faced while trying to keep the aircraft under control.
The suicidal Omani co-pilot al-Hammami attacked Machchar with an axe kept in the cockpit, causing a "depressed fracture fragment of skull".
Despite suffering severe injuries, the Indian pilot ensured the situation did not escalate and thwarted the Omani co-pilot’s alleged 9/11-style attack.

stories.headline: 'Will call Putin over pneumonic plague,' says Trump - what is happening in Russia?
stories.deck: A woman at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia reportedly died from pneumonia of unknown cause. While there are suggestions she may have contracted pneumonic plague, Russian authorities have not confirmed this diagnosis. The World Health Organisation assesses the risk of spreading beyond Russia as very low and is in contact with Russian officials. US President Donald Trump plans…
stories.bodyText:
Reports of a case of pneumonic plague at a research institute in Siberia have triggered international concern, with US president Donald Trump saying he plans to speak with Russian president Vladimir Putin about the case even as the World Health Organisation says the risk beyond Russia remains “very low”.
The case emerged after a woman working at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East died last week. Russian authorities said she had pneumonia of unknown cause, while reports in Russian media and on social media suggested she may have contracted pneumonic plague.
There is, however, no confirmation that the woman died of plague.
The WHO said Tuesday that it was in contact with Russian authorities following reports of her death. Russian officials told the agency that no case of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk and that tests had found no dangerous infectious pathogens among people who had been in contact with the woman.
Why did the case raise alarms
Pneumonic plague is the least common but most virulent form of plague and affects the lungs. Unlike bubonic plague, which is generally transmitted through infected fleas, pneumonic plague can spread between people through respiratory particles.
The disease can become fatal if untreated, but WHO says recovery rates are high when it is detected and treated promptly. Symptoms can include shortness of breath and coughing, sometimes with blood.
The possibility of a respiratory disease emerging from a laboratory has also revived memories of the Covid-19 pandemic and the debate over its origins. WHO spokesman Christian Lindmeier stressed that there was currently no indication that the Siberian case was comparable to the pandemic.
“There is currently no indication that we are dealing with anything similar to the pandemic,” Lindmeier told news agency AP.
The institute where the woman worked studies dangerous pathogens, including plague, in a region where the disease occurs naturally among wild animals.
What Russia is saying
Russian health authorities said they had carried out preventive measures including contact tracing, medical monitoring and laboratory testing.
According to a health alert relayed to AP by WHO, tests found no dangerous infectious disease pathogens among the woman's contacts. Authorities said medical monitoring of all contacts had also been completed and that the epidemiological situation remained stable.
Russian officials have pushed back against speculation surrounding the death. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged the public to rely on statements from Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, rather than “rumors or speculation”.
Russian media reports have offered different accounts of how the woman may have become ill, including an alleged laboratory accident involving a test tube containing live bacteria. Another report suggested a possible link to travel. There is no public evidence supporting those theories, and Russia's health watchdog rejected the laboratory-accident account.
Trump, Rubio seek more information
Trump said he was due to speak with Putin about the case “very soon” and said the US was engaged in “very deep discussions” on the issue.
He had earlier offered to help Russia, describing plague as a disease that had once been controllable but saying microbes had become “stronger and smarter”.
Secretary of state Marco Rubio also urged Moscow to provide more information.
“Maybe there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” Rubio said, calling on Russia to be more transparent and share information with the international community.
The Kremlin said it welcomed offers of assistance but referred questions about the case to Rospotrebnadzor.
How dangerous is pneumonic plague?
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and still occurs naturally in parts of the world, including Siberia.
Pneumonic plague is particularly concerning because it can be transmitted through respiratory particles. But experts quoted by AP said the bacteria do not spread easily over long distances, and modern antibiotics can prevent the disease from becoming a wider threat when cases are detected quickly.
WHO has said the risk outside Russia is currently “very low”.
The Irkutsk institute, established in 1934, was created to control plague outbreaks in Siberia and the Far East and has since worked on other dangerous diseases including cholera and anthrax.

stories.headline: Problems are, in reality, a matter of choice
stories.deck: Problems are, in reality, a matter of choice
stories.bodyText: With the onset of adolescence come more problems between parents and teenagers, most commonly expressed in the form of complaints. There are problems stemming from adolescent separation. Parents complain about teenagers’ lack of interaction, while teenagers complain of parental interference. . What is a problem anyway? It is a perceived discrepancy between how things are and how one would like them to be. A problem is just a judgement call. . It is the dissatisfaction created by an identified problem that can drive efforts to close the discrepancy and restore personal contentment. In this sense, problems come with their own motivation to resolve them. This dissatisfaction can range from mild upset (‘I misplaced my keys’) to major pain (‘I hate how I am being treated’). . Because a problem is a judgement call, it is always a matter of choice: whether or not to take issue with some conduct, circumstance or condition. And here conflicts can arise between parent and teenager, and between parents, over whether something should be treated as a problem or not. .Psychological trauma: The scars we don’t name. For example, consider parent-teenager conflict. Take the messy room that parents consider a problem, but the teenager does not. Then there are situations where the teenager’s behaviour is deemed a problem by one parent but not the other, creating conflict between the two adults. Then there are controlling parents who are too critical of their adolescent children. . The more judgemental, rigid and demanding a parent is, the more problems that adult will choose to have with the adolescent. The more accepting, flexible and adaptive a parent is, the fewer problems that adult will choose to have with the adolescent. Adolescents need both acceptance and correction, and it helps the family if each parent is a source of both. . When it comes to fixing a problem, there are really only three paths to resolution: 1) Change things to become how you would like them to be; 2) change what you want to accept; and 3) compromise: change some and accept some as they are. . Here, the contribution of laughter, enjoyment, play, fun, expressions of interest and love is essential to help renew and restore a relationship that is faring badly at the moment.

stories.headline: Blood-tainted ice cubes and a famine in Madras
stories.deck: The Ice House remains a popular reminder of a place where the British sold ice. Behind that luxury, however, lay a darker history of labour, exploitation, and suffering
stories.bodyText:
In the sweltering heat of colonial Madras, British rulers and the city’s elite raised glasses of Scotch whisky, chilled by ice cubes floating in their drinks.
The huge blocks of ice were naturally formed in the lakes of New England in the U.S. and imported to India. In Madras (now Chennai), the ice bars were brought to the Ice House in Triplicane, where they were stored and cut into smaller pieces for evening drinks.
The Ice House, even today, remains a popular reminder of a place where the British sold ice. Behind that luxury, however, lay a darker history of labour, exploitation, and suffering.
A tale of exploitation
The story of the ice was also the story of the workers who handled it. Scheduled Caste (SC) labourers were employed to cut, move, and handle the massive blocks under punishing conditions. Tamil writer Jeyamohan brings this little-known world alive in his novel Vellai Yaanai, set against the backdrop of the Great Madras Famine of 1876-78, which wiped half the SC population. The book is translated in English as White Elephant by Priyamvada Ramkumar.
The novel is part-fact and part-fiction. Jeyamohan said the idea came to him during a conversation with the late Anbu Ponnoviyam, a scholar belonging to an SC community, who told him about “a protest that took place during the Great Madras Famine at the Ice House – a protest by and for the Dalit workers.”
Drawing on oral accounts and historical material, he sought to reconstruct the experiences of workers and an episode of labour unrest that, he argues, has received little attention in conventional histories of Madras.
“The White Elephant” is a metaphor for the giant blocks of ice imported from America. Jeyamohan has described the novel as “a war against India’s historical amnesia and amnesias that sculpt our everyday lives.”
Oppression and resistance
Present-day Chennai knows Vivekananda House and remembers it by its earlier name, Ice House; yet the history associated with it is largely outside the city’s popular memory.
Built in 1842 by Frederic Tudor, the Ice House was used to store naturally formed ice cut from lakes in New England and shipped across the seas to India.
The ice blocks, packed with insulating material such as sawdust, wood shavings, or rice chaff, were a remarkable example of a colonial-era trade in a commodity that was otherwise unavailable in the tropics.
Jeyamohan’s protagonist, Aiden Byrne, is an Irish police officer in Madras. His encounter with two labourers employed by the Tudor Ice Company mercilessly beaten in the countryside forces him to confront the brutality of the imperial system of which he is a part. He inspects the Ice House with his platoon and is appalled by the conditions in which the workers are made to labour.
In the novel, the workers handle the ice in darkness and with little protection. Working in the abysmal conditions left the workers with “ash-like lesions, open sores and peeling skin on their fingers and toes. Their legs were bent and twisted in myriad ways, resembling a strange thicket of thorns,” writes Jeyamohan.
The blocks themselves are described as weighing as much as “30 tonnes – the weight of ten elephants” and sliding unpredictably when unpacked. “The White Elephant rumbled, lowered its crown, and moved forward, baying for blood. The workers shrieked in panic,” describes the novel.
Jeyamohan places this story of labour exploitation alongside the devastation of the Great Madras Famine. Aiden travels to witness the migration of the SCs from Chengalpattu towards Madras and encounters the full horror of famine – bodies lying by the roadside, many of them children, with people starving and reduced to begging for food.
Everything Aiden has witnessed so far begins to make him question the imperial order he serves. With the help of Kathavarayan, a young activist from the oppressed community, he organises the workers at the Ice factory to demand better working conditions for them.
The character Kathavarayan is based on the historical figure Pandit Iyothee Thass, whose original name was Kathavarayan.
Iyothee Thass’ influence
Jeyamohan has deliberately chosen the real character of Pandit Iyothee Thass, an SC scholar. Here, however, the boundary between history and fiction becomes important.
Iyothee Thass was also a Siddha practitioner, Buddhist revivalist, and social reformer. He lived in Royapettah and later emerged as one of the most important voices challenging caste hierarchy and the social exclusion of the Paraiyars and other oppressed communities.
But there is no established historical evidence that Iyothee Thass organised workers against the Tudor Ice Company or played a role in a trade union movement involving its SC labourers. That part of Vellai Yaanai is Jeyamohan’s fictional reconstruction.
The distinction is particularly significant because Iyothee Thass was known personally to several prominent figures of the period.
Tamil scholar and trade union leader Thiru. Vi. Kalyanasundaram, popularly known as Thiru-Vi-Ka, was familiar with him. Yet, in his autobiographical writings, Thiru-Vi-Ka makes no reference to any trade union activities by Iyothee Thass.
What he does record is Iyothee Thass’s reputation as a Siddha practitioner. Recalling ailments he suffered during his youth, Thiru-Vi-Ka describes how Iyothee Thass successfully treated him on more than one occasion, including an injury to his hand sustained while breaking coconuts during a festival.
There is, however, a striking historical parallel between the fictional Kathavarayan’s rejection of Hinduism and Iyothee Thass’s own intellectual journey.
Iyothee Thass’s encounter with caste discrimination led him away from Vaishnavism towards Buddhism. In the novel, Aiden is puzzled to see Kathavarayan without the usual Vaishnavite mark on his forehead.
Kathavarayan says he has “renounced” it and “the religion, the god, and all the associated identities.”
Pandit Iyothee Thass met Theosophist Colonel H.S. Olcott and expressed his desire to embrace Buddhism. With Olcott’s assistance, he travelled to Ceylon and, on his return, helped establish the Sakya Buddhist Society, also known as the Indian Buddhist Association, in Madras in 1898.
The movement established a presence in Royapettah and became a centre for the study and propagation of Buddhism. Thiru-Vi-Ka, in his writings, recalls listening to Buddhist teachings, including lessons on the Tripitaka. He also records the opposition the movement encountered because of its criticism of established religious traditions.
Thus, even where Jeyamohan fictionalises the historical record, the novel draws upon a genuine historical transformation: that of a man who confronted caste oppression and eventually sought an alternative intellectual and religious tradition in Buddhism.
The novel seeks to remind the people of Chennai of the real story behind the Ice House and of Pandit Iyothee Thass, the scholar who walked the length and breadth of the city, wrote and preached, yet remains known only to a few.

stories.headline: The perils of gated learning: Why pushing Humanities out of IITs risks erasing critical citizenship
stories.bodyText: The recent suicide of Sahil Wakode, a 22-year-old Dalit student enrolled in IIT Bombay, has, not surprisingly, led to a demand for liquidating humanities and social sciences (HSS) from these ‘Institutions of Eminence’. This deep unease regarding the presence of HSS in IITs found among alumni, a resounding majority of the faculty, industry experts, tech giants, and other ‘concerned’ citizens is no new development. For decades, it has been expressed in the name of safeguarding the core objective of IITs. . These ‘well-wishers’ of IITs assert that an institutional landscape envisioned for and committed to STEM education and research should not include HSS, as their presence necessarily pollutes the eminence and distinction these institutes have arduously built over the decades. The concern primarily has to do with the dilution of a certain IIT vibe. However, the question arises, how did these allegedly lesser sciences make it to the upper echelons of higher education, ones reserved for more eminent domains of inquiry? . Commenting on the kind of technical education needed in a country like India, the 1945 Sarkar Committee emphasised the importance of ‘development of character, outlook, and mental ability in a student so that he may become a useful citizen’. Its report further underlined the necessity of providing ‘a combination of a fundamental scientific training with a broad human outlook’. Engineering as a domain was seen as exceedingly crucial to nation-building. For this reason, it could not be reduced to technical training and industry exposure. It had to offer an authentic educational experience, in the sense of being present in a more informed and responsible manner. Therefore, right from the beginning, HSS were an integral part of IITs. .IIT Bombay likely to discuss new rules for exam misconduct this week following student suicide. The early visionaries of engineering education did not identify the students in these institutes as mere job aspirants perpetually learning the tricks of the game to stay in the race. The engineering student was seen as a budding citizen, one who had to be initiated into a constitutionally informed sense of associated living. So the usefulness of HSS was nurturing socially informed engineers, ones who knew the societal context in which their engineering education took place. Rescued from the conventional narrowness of technical education, these engineers were to play a vital role in building a modern India, one that prized growth and development beyond and above material and infrastructural progress. . Making them ‘great’ again . Polish-British sociologist Zygmunt Bauman’s celebrated works offer an insightful reading of the dark side of modern rational decision-making. His invocation of the metaphor “gardening state” – a significant addition in the sociology of genocide – seems apt even today as fascist politics stifles the essentials of democracy one after another, labeling them as threats. Free-floating animalistic metaphors such as “termites” and “cockroaches”, often deployed to designate the “unwanted” in society, serve as a manual for action. The end goal is to remove, delete, cut, eliminate, and clean the national space. NRC and SIR also operate in a similar logic of cleaning the nation’s garden. . In the context of IITs, HSS are seen as ‘undesirable’ weeds that need ‘weeding’ from these alleged gardens of ‘eminence’. The populist, careerist, and neoliberal flag-bearers express unease over HSS courses being taught to ‘meritorious’, ‘bright’ students, suggesting the courses pollute or corrupt their minds. So removing and liquidating such disciplines is increasingly seen as a final solution. Such a suggestively arrogant appeal to liquidate social sciences is also seen in the West. . The grievance of the self-proclaimed well-wishers of IITs suggests a ‘once upon a time HSS-less IIT’ phase. The premise is that back in those wonderful days, these centres of excellence were doing exceptionally well, and then, HSS arrived as a disruptive and unwanted addition to an otherwise fantastic learning space. Thus, the ‘make IITs great again’ argument boils down to the most reasonable remedy: push HSS out of these centres of excellence so that they can get back on track. Needless to mention, this is also a testament to their peerless ignorance of the history of engineering education. They are blissfully unaware, even indifferent, to the losses we will incur when the slate is wiped clean. . Given their markedly shallow understanding of engineering education in India, it should not be surprising that their understanding of greatness is unsettlingly narrow. We must ask what accounts for IITs’ greatness and whether it has anything to do with these ‘well-wishers’. . The writers teach at the Indian Institute of Management, Kozhikode. . (Disclaimer: The views expressed above are the author's own. They do not necessarily reflect the views of DH.)

briefs.headline: 3 years after October 7, Israel remembers its dead amid election heat
briefs.bodyText:
Israel on Wednesday marked the third anniversary of Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack, with memorial events being held across the country as the anniversary coincides with preparations for a general election.
The commemorations are the first since a ceasefire began in Gaza last year. Families and communities are remembering those killed and taken hostage during the assault, which remains a defining event in Israeli politics and security.
The attack began at 6.29am, when Palestinian fighters breached the Gaza border and attacked southern Israeli communities with guns, rockets and grenades. According to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures, 1,221 people were killed and 251 hostages were taken to Gaza. Forty-four of the hostages were already dead.
A memorial was scheduled at Kibbutz Kfar Aza at the exact time the attack began. Sixty-four residents were killed and 18 people were abducted from the community. Another ceremony was planned at the site of the Nova music festival, where more than 370 people were killed and dozens were taken hostage.
Bereaved families were also due to gather at a Tel Aviv park on Wednesday evening.
Israel on high alert
Security has been tightened for the commemorations, which come three weeks before Israel's general election and a week after a foiled attack on a passenger plane bound for Tel Aviv.
Israel's defence minister said the military had been placed on high alert "in light of intelligence regarding Hamas's intentions to attempt to carry out attacks" against troops in Gaza on the anniversary.
At state memorial ceremonies on Monday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said there would be no Hamas rule in Gaza and vowed to continue targeting those involved in the October 7 attack or those who held hostages.
Israel's military campaign in Gaza, launched after the Hamas attack, has killed more than 74,200 Palestinians, according to Gaza's health ministry. The offensive has also devastated large parts of the enclave.
The conflict subsequently expanded beyond Gaza, with Israel fighting Hezbollah in Lebanon and confronting Iran as its military operations widened across the region.
Gaza remains unresolved
The ceasefire has not ended the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians continue to live in tents or temporary shelters, while plans for reconstruction and the territory's future governance remain uncertain.
Israel says it controls more than 60% of Gaza and has continued carrying out airstrikes, saying they target Hamas and those involved in the October 7 attack.
Gaza's health ministry says more than 1,430 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces since the ceasefire began.
With elections approaching, the October 7 attack and its aftermath are expected to remain central to Israel's political debate.

briefs.headline: Grandfather shoots lawyer grandson dead: How blood splatters exposed killing
briefs.deck: Abhay Marathe, a 33-year-old lawyer, was found dead from a bullet injury in Lonavla. His family initially claimed the shooting was accidental while he cleaned his grandfather's rifle. However, police investigation revealed inconsistencies and evidence of a dispute over property. Abhay's grandfather Motiram Marathe has been charged with murder, and four relatives are accused of destroying evidence.
briefs.bodyText:
PUNE: A family’s account of a Lonavla lawyer’s death as an accidental shooting began to unravel after police examining his body found that the bullet wound did not appear consistent with the version they had been given.
The discovery led investigators to the hotel where 33-year-old lawyer Abhay Marathe was allegedly shot dead during a dispute over the sale of a property, police said.
His 83-year-old grandfather, Motiram Marathe, was arrested on Monday on the charge of murder. Four other relatives were arrested for allegedly destroying evidence, Pune Rural police said.
What happened at the hotel
Lonavla City police were alerted by a hospital on Monday afternoon that Abhay, from Bhushi, had died from a bullet injury.
His family told doctors and police that he had been cleaning Motiram’s 12-bore rifle inside their hotel when it accidentally went off. The bullet hit Abhay in the chest, killing him instantly.
Police initially registered an accidental death case.
But when Abhay’s body was sent to Sassoon General Hospital in Pune for post-mortem, Superintendent of Police (Pune Rural) Sandeep Singh Gill, additional superintendent Shubham Kumar and local crime branch inspector Pramod Kshirsagar examined the injury.
“Self-inflicted or accidental firearm injuries are different from the injury we found on Abhay. In an accidental firing, it is unlikely for a rifle bullet to hit the chest,” Gill said.
Blood stains raised further questions
The crime branch then went to the hotel where the shooting was said to have taken place.
Investigators found a pool of blood on the wall beside the hotel counter and another pool nearby. Blood splatters were also visible on a wall about five feet above the ground.
“This increased our suspicion that Abhay was shot dead inside the hotel,” Gill said.
Police questioned the hotel workers and manager, who told them about a dispute between Abhay and his grandfather over the sale of a property.
Dispute over property sale
Motiram had opposed the sale of the property, police said.
“They again had a heated argument over the issue around 11.30am on Monday. Abhay allegedly charged at his grandfather during the argument. Motiram then took out his licensed rifle and shot his grandson dead,” Gill said.
Police allege that the family then tried to make the shooting appear accidental.
CCTV cameras allegedly removed
Gill said Abhay’s sister, uncle, aunt and cousin were alerted after the shooting and came to the hotel.
They allegedly moved Abhay’s body into one of the rooms before removing the CCTV cameras and digital video recorder (DVR) and hiding them.
“They threatened the hotel employees against revealing anything. Thereafter, they informed Abhay’s parents about the incident,” Gill said. The four relatives — Rajashri Pawar, 58; Hiraman Marathe, 54; Kavita Marathe, Hiraman’s wife; and Manoj Marathe, 32 — were arrested for allegedly destroying evidence.
Two licensed rifles
Police said Motiram had two licensed rifles. He obtained the licences in 1970 for hunting.
The accused have been charged under sections 103 (murder), 238 (causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen offender) and 241 (destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with sections of the Indian Arms Act.

briefs.headline: 'Islam wanting to take over': Donald Trump reacts to France school protests
briefs.bodyText:
US President 
Donald Trump
 on Wednesday reacted to growing student protests in France, claiming the demonstrations reflected “mass migration” and saying they were about “Islam wanting to take over” the country.
“What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
More than 266,000 people took part in nationwide demonstrations on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, according to France’s Interior Ministry. The protests, which began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September, have spread across the country as students demand more funding for education.
Police fired tear gas and clashed with small groups of protesters in Paris after an otherwise largely peaceful march. Nearly 500 people were detained, the ministry said.
Students have been blockading schools and boycotting classes for more than two weeks. Police have made more than 6,500 arrests since the protests began, most involving minors, according to officials.
The use of tear gas, batons and other riot-control weapons against teenagers has drawn criticism from students, parents and teachers. 
Some student groups have called for further protests on Thursday.
French interior minister Laurent Nuñez defended the police response, saying it had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and that officers had intervened when protests turned violent.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school authorities needed to listen to students and address their concerns. He also condemned what he called “ultra violence” around schools and rejected allegations of racism in the police response as a “lie”.
The protests have become an early flashpoint in France’s presidential election campaign, amid wider anger over public spending, poverty and wealth inequality. Rising fuel prices linked to the Iran war have added to the discontent.
Felix Barney, a university student, criticised the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make “any sense to hit minors.”
The latest tensions also come after a 15-year-old boy lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade on Monday. Nuñez said 715 police officers had been injured during the unrest.

briefs.headline: Messi's emotional farewell ends in 1 goal, 2 assists and 3-0 win for Argentina
briefs.deck: Lionel Messi’s emotional Argentina farewell ended in a 3-0 victory over Benin at the Monumental. After an extraordinary pre-match tribute, Messi assisted Nicolás Otamendi’s opener and Nico Paz’s curling finish before scoring a penalty himself. He came close again late on, hitting the post, before sending a final free-kick over the bar as Argentina celebrated a memorable night.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Lionel Messi
’s final appearance for Argentina ended with victory, emotion and one last unforgettable night at the Monumental as the South American side defeated Benin 3-0 on Wednesday.
The occasion was as much about Messi as the result. The stadium was packed long before kick-off, with the Argentine captain receiving an extraordinary farewell.
Fabio Santana, a Malvinas War veteran and singer, performed the Argentine national anthem as Messi stood alongside his children, visibly emotional. A giant Messi shirt covered the pitch before the crowd erupted into a rendition of “Muchachos”.
At the 10-minute mark, the match paused for another tribute, with every Benin player taking the opportunity to shake Messi’s hand.
Argentina dominated possession early and repeatedly tried to find their captain in dangerous positions. Messi came close with a free-kick from outside the box, but Benin’s goalkeeper made a fine save.
Lautaro Martínez also threatened after a run into the area, while another Messi pass nearly released him into space. Benin, however, refused to sit back completely and gradually grew into the contest.
They eventually switched to a back five, with Messi receiving close attention whenever he came near the penalty area.
As it happened: 
Argentina vs Benin Highlights
Messi's assist prompts opener
The breakthrough finally arrived shortly after half-time. Julián Álvarez won a corner after bursting down the left, and Messi delivered the set-piece perfectly.
Nicolás Otamendi, left completely unmarked, volleyed home to put Argentina ahead. It was a fitting goal for the veteran defender, who was also making his final appearance for the national team.
Argentina doubled their advantage through Nico Paz. The youngster, who had just come onto the pitch as a substitute, collected the ball and produced a beautiful left-footed curling finish, drawing comparisons with Messi’s trademark style.
Messi on the scoresheet
Messi was involved again, providing the assist as Paz announced himself on the biggest stage.
Then came the moment everyone inside the Monumental had been waiting for. Messi stepped up from the penalty spot and calmly sent the goalkeeper the wrong way, placing the ball into the top-right corner for 3-0.
There was still time for one final glimpse of magic. Messi had a late effort saved before another strike hit the post, and in the dying seconds he won a free-kick in his familiar range. He took responsibility one last time, but the effort sailed over the crossbar.
The whistle confirmed Argentina’s 3-0 victory. For Messi, though, the scoreline was almost secondary. The night belonged to the boy from Rosario who became Argentina’s greatest footballer, and who finally said goodbye to the shirt he made his own.

briefs.headline: A snack worth a little spanking
briefs.deck: A snack worth a little spanking
briefs.bodyText: ‘Chana jor garam, babu, mein laya majedar, chana jor garam!’ The melodious call of my favourite street hawker breaks into my afternoon siesta. He would materialise promptly at 4 o’clock, carrying a basket containing his delectable savouries made out of ground chanagram. Tea time could never be complete without his lip-smacking, mouth-watering snacks. My tongue would start salivating the moment I saw him walk into our lane. He was always dressed in a spotless dhoti and banyan, which soon sported a layer of oil as the evening wore on. . He would modulate his sales pitch to catch our attention. In no time, he would be surrounded by his clientele, like a swarm of homing bees humming in their hive. Every single grain of gram in his stock was carefully roasted and fried to tickle our tongues and let us share in his heavenly savouries. . Mechanically, but with great finesse, he mixed the roasted grams, fresh coriander leaves, finely chopped onions, puffed rice, green chilli, sev and various other ingredients, both sweet and sour. He would tear out a page from yesterday’s newspaper and roll it into a cone-shaped container. He would then pour the chana-jor into the cone. The final touch came from his secret, a green chutney or a squeeze of lemon. My fingers would twitch with excitement when he handed over the cone-shaped cup of chana-jor. .Odette’s Chef-owner Julien Royer interview: ‘A customer named her baby after our restaurant’. The paper, which was crisp and virgin to start with, was soon smeared with oil and crumpled beyond recognition. Even Hercule Poirot would have found it an onerous task to decipher the ingredients therefrom. . My chana man travelled light. His entire universe was contained within the caddies he carried with him. He had no regular shop nor a fixed address. He simply parked his cycle by the roadside and announced his presence with his signature tune: ‘Chana jor garam…’ . Young and old, boys and girls, truants and the studious, all rushed to him for their snack. We were not deterred by our parents’ warnings about the unhygienic nature of such ‘forbidden’ food. The ‘kick’ delivered by the spicy chana jor was so fiery that a blow or two from my father on my posterior was of little consequence in deterring me — a small price to pay for the bliss of enjoying garma garam chana masala!

briefs.headline: As the US govt wants to change the clock 'forever', researchers in Canada warn
briefs.deck: The push for making Daylight Saving Time permanent is gaining momentum in the U.S., bolstered by President Trump. Nevertheless, this move is met with pushback because of health-related concerns brought to light by recent studies. Experts warn that this change could interfere with natural circadian rhythms, posing potential health risks.
briefs.bodyText:
A renewed political drive in the United States to end seasonal clock adjustments by locking in year-round Daylight Saving Time is facing resistance from both Capitol Hill and the medical community. While President Donald Trump has put heavy pressure on lawmakers to pass the measure -- calling for extra evening sunshine for recreation and business -- a growing body of scientific evidence warns that the policy could trigger chronic public health damage. Incidentally, some members of Congress in the US have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill in 2022 to make daylight saving time permanent, but it got stalled in the House.
The debate reignited this week with the publication of a research review in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. As several Canadian jurisdictions weigh ending their own clock changes, researchers examined the physiological fallout of permanent daylight saving time compared to permanent standard time. 
Their findings endorse permanent standard time as the healthier option, cautioning that extended evening light paired with darker winter mornings runs counter to the fundamental biology of the human body. For those unaware, Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the US are set one hour ahead of standard time.
Why researchers are against 'changing' the clock
According to the authors of the research report, the human circadian rhythm runs on a natural cycle of roughly 24.2 hours and relies critically on natural morning sunlight to reset and synchronize essential bodily functions. While later daylight hours may accommodate evening commutes and outdoor leisure, delayed sunrise suppresses natural wakefulness. Conversely, lingering evening light delays the internal clock, disrupting sleep quality, mood, and daily productivity.
The consequences of late-shifted sunlight are already visible along the geographic borders of current time zones, where sunrise and sunset can vary by over an hour within a single zone. The Canadian review cited evidence showing that Americans living on the western edges of time zones -- where the sun sets later -- lose roughly an hour of sleep each week compared to those on the eastern side. The researchers concluded that while abolishing biannual clock adjustments eliminates a few weeks of acute disruption each year, the consequences of permanent daylight saving time would be chronic. Their recommendation aligns with broad consensus across international chronobiology and sleep medicine organizations, including a 2024 guidance from British sleep specialists advocating a permanent lock on Greenwich Mean Time.
Permanent daylight bill: Where it stands right now
Called the Sunshine Protection Act, it passed in the House in July this year, but faces roadblocks in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including President Trump and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Those against, say that permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings.
Despite these warnings, legislative momentum in Washington remains contentious. While the U.S. House of Representatives has advanced a measure establishing permanent daylight saving time, the bill has stalled in the Senate. The impasse even prompted President Trump to escalate public pressure, going so far as to post the personal mobile phone number of Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas on social media.
Defending his stance, Cotton noted that previous attempts to lock the clock to summer hours collapsed once citizens faced the reality of dark winter mornings. Historical records support the pushback: the United States previously adopted permanent daylight saving time during World War II and again during the 1973 energy crisis, with Congress repealing the 1970s initiative after less than a year amid intense public outcry over morning darkness. Similar nationwide trials in Russia and Chile were also later reversed due to public dissatisfaction, safety concerns, and body-clock disruption.
Canadian researchers further note that a permanent shift by the United States would place severe economic pressure on Canada to follow suit, regardless of medical advice.

stories.headline: Problem solved or buried? Bengaluru road turns ‘natural tunnel’ after rain; officials fill it with debris in bizarre fix
stories.deck: A significant cavity formed on Kanteerava Studio Main Road in Bengaluru after heavy rainfall. A reporter climbed inside the cavity to highlight the road's danger as traffic passed by. Residents expressed concerns about the road's deteriorating condition even before the rains exacerbated the situation. Civic officials plan to asphalt the road after temporary filling, following complications from…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: A television reporter literally climbed inside a Bengaluru road to demonstrate how dangerous a giant cavity had become — and the bizarre sight exposed a “natural tunnel” running underneath the carriageway.
The cavity opened up on Kanteerava Studio Main Road after two days of heavy rain. Instead of remaining a conventional pothole, the road had given way from underneath, leaving a hollow passage beneath the surface.
The reporter was able to sit inside the cavity as motorists carefully squeezed past the damaged portion. The video quickly drew attention online, with commuters and opposition leaders questioning the condition of Bengaluru’s roads.
The underground cavity was created as rainwater, unable to drain properly, began flowing beneath the road. The force of the water eroded the soil and road structure as it moved towards a manhole, effectively carving out a tunnel below the carriageway.
And the immediate solution? Officials began filling the cavity with broken concrete blocks and construction debris.
When TOI visited the spot on Tuesday evening, the filling work was still in progress, while traffic continued to move around the damaged portion.
The incident has brought renewed attention to the condition of the less-than-one-kilometre stretch between Surana College and Nandini Layout. The road is a key link between residential neighbourhoods and the Peenya and Yeshwanthpur industrial belts and carries heavy traffic every day.
Residents said the stretch had been deteriorating long before the latest rains. They alleged that repeated digging by utility agencies and inadequate restoration had left several portions of the road vulnerable.
“This did not happen overnight. The road has been in bad shape for years, and the rains only made things worse,” said Deepak Gowda, a regular commuter. He said the pothole was visible on Monday but became much deeper after the heavy rain.
For motorists, the problem is not limited to the monsoon. Shwetha R, who travels to Nagarbhavi daily for work, said the stretch is dusty in dry weather and hazardous when it rains.
“When the weather is dry, the stretch is extremely dusty. During the rains, motorists cannot even judge the depth of the potholes. Filling them with construction debris is not a solution — it only creates another uneven surface,” she said.
Naveen Kumara M, a Kamakshipalya resident who regularly uses the road on his two-wheeler, said the condition was particularly surprising given the importance of the route.
“This is a major access road to the Peenya industrial area. Thousands of people use it every day, yet the road looks abandoned. People keep asking what it will take for the authorities to asphalt even this short stretch,” he said.
Some commuters said they had begun taking longer routes to avoid the damaged corridor.
Gowda said residents had repeatedly escalated complaints about the road.
“I am tired of even complaining about this stretch. It is just irritating. Look at that pothole. Are we even living in Bengaluru? I have been escalating the matter from the corporation to the CM and the chief secretary. Forget normal two-wheelers and cars — not even off-roading vehicles can survive this stretch. We are absolutely sick of it,” he said.
Bengaluru West City Corporation commissioner Rajendra KV said the civic body had already approved funds for the road under the Special Infrastructure Project and was preparing to asphalt it.
The plan, however, had been complicated by B-Smile (Bengaluru Smart Infrastructure Limited), which had proposed taking up the stretch for whitetopping.
“We were almost ready to start the asphalting when B-Smile intervened, saying it would take up the road for whitetopping. However, following today’s incident, we have told B-Smile to take up the whitetopping after three to four years, while we will proceed with asphalting now. Once the rains subside, we will take up the asphalting work at the earliest,” Rajendra said.
B-Smile director (technical) BS Prahlad did not respond to calls or messages from TOI.

stories.headline: Rental scam: Online property enquiry leaves Bengaluru woman Rs 21 lakh poorer
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A 24-year-old private-sector employee lost a staggering Rs 21.1 lakh after an online search for a rental property in Banaswadi led her into a carefully orchestrated scam.
Two fraudsters allegedly posed as the property owner and society manager, repeatedly demanding money on various pretexts, including a visiting pass, verification charges, rent, security deposit, and “refundable” fees. Trusting the purported rental deal, the woman continued making payments, only to realise she had fallen victim to a massive financial fraud.
According to the complaint filed by 
Prerana
 (name changed), she contacted a person regarding a rental property listed on a real estate platform on Sept 25. The post had details of the property along with photographs. The person later called and introduced himself as property owner Dr Ameya. He told Prerana that a visiting pass was required and that Rs 22,000 had to be paid along with identity proof to visit the property. Trusting him, she shared her ID and initially paid Rs 2,000.
The following day, Dr Ameya told her that the society manager would contact her. Shortly afterwards, a person identifying himself as Vijay Kale contacted her on 
WhatsApp
 and claimed to be the society manager. Kale asked her to complete certain forms and pay Rs 28,099, saying Rs 28,000 would be refunded and Rs 299 was a machine charge. 
Prerana made the payment. Kale then claimed that the transaction had been made incorrectly and instructed her to make separate payments of Rs 28,000 and Rs 299, which she again paid.
The demands continued under the guise of completing the rental formalities. Kale asked for rent and deposit receipts and assured her that the amounts would be refunded immediately after the procedures. She paid Rs 15,000 towards rent and Rs 2.3 lakh as deposit.
She was subsequently asked to arrange a little over Rs 2.4 lakh. Since her transaction limit prevented her from making further payments, Rs 2.2 lakh was arranged from her father’s bank account, while a friend paid Rs 15,000 on her behalf. After receiving Rs 21.1 lakh in total, Kale again demanded another Rs 2.2 lakh, claiming that the visiting pass and refund process would not be completed otherwise. It was at this stage that the woman stopped making payments and realised she had been duped.
Prerana immediately contacted the cyber helpline, 1930, and reported the fraud. Later, she lodged a complaint with East cybercrime police station and submitted bank statements, digital payment transaction details, along with screenshots of WhatsApp conversations and calls, details of the persons involved, mobile numbers and portal property information. Her friend has separately reported the fraudulent transaction to the Telangana cybercrime authorities.
She said Dr Ameya used mobile no. 8076759133 and Vijay Kale used no. 8882486410. The transactions and communications took place between 10.43 pm on Sept 25 and 2.31 pm on Sept 26. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act and Section 318 (cheating) of BNS.

stories.headline: Cabinet approves five commissionerates for Bengaluru; former officers express concern
stories.deck: Former senior police officers have questioned whether a civic structure can be directly replicated in policing, arguing that crime, law and order, traffic management and emergency mobilisation do not necessarily follow municipal boundaries
stories.bodyText:
The Karnataka Cabinet on Tuesday approved the reorganisation of the Bengaluru police commissionerate into five commissionerates, with a Chief Police Commissioner to oversee them.
The proposed overhaul has triggered a sharp debate among serving and retired police officials.
The restructuring has been proposed against the backdrop of Bengaluru’s rapid expansion and the creation of the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA), which has divided the civic administration into five corporations. The proposed police model broadly seeks to mirror this arrangement to improve coordination between the police and civic authorities.
However, former senior police officers have questioned whether a civic structure can be directly replicated in policing, arguing that crime, law and order, traffic management and emergency mobilisation do not necessarily follow municipal boundaries.
A former DGP who served in the Bengaluru city police said the proposed arrangement could create more problems than solutions, particularly in operational policing. According to the former officer, the proposal appears to be driven partly by the desire to “accommodate senior officials seeking postings in major metropolitan centres rather than by a clearly established operational requirement”.
‘Existing command structure could be weakened’
The former DGP said the present city police structure has a clearly defined chain of command involving the Commissioner of Police, DCPs, inspectors and constables, with responsibilities and jurisdictions understood at every level. The proposed five-commissionerate system, he argued, could dilute this established structure by creating multiple command centres and overlapping responsibilities.
“The existing system has a clear chain of command. The new arrangement could make these established positions less significant and create confusion at different levels,” the former officer said.
He also warned that the mobilisation of police forces during major emergencies could become considerably more difficult. At present, the city police commissioner can mobilise forces across the entire city depending on the requirement. Under a five-commissionerate system, however, the deployment of personnel across jurisdictions could require greater coordination between several commissioners and their establishments, he said.
VIP movements could expose coordination problems
The former DGP cited the movement of high-profile dignitaries as an example.
At present, when the Prime Minister, President or other VVIPs visit Bengaluru, the city police commissioner can coordinate security and traffic arrangements across the entire route.
Under the proposed system, if a convoy passes through multiple commissionerates, each commissionerate could be required to coordinate and deploy its own personnel. The officer said this could result in duplication of manpower and unnecessary deployment of specialised units.
He cited the example of the City Armed Reserve (CAR) units, which are currently deployed and coordinated through the existing city police structure for escort and security duties.
Under the proposed arrangement, individual commissionerates could be required to deploy personnel and resources for the portions of the movement falling within their respective jurisdictions, potentially resulting in duplication of deployment and coordination.
‘Why create five establishments?’
The former officer also questioned the financial implications of creating five separate commissionerates.
Apart from the proposed 6,000 additional posts, the government would have to provide office infrastructure, vehicles, communication systems, accommodation, administrative staff and other facilities for the new establishments. The infrastructure requirement alone, he said, could impose a significant additional financial burden on the government.
“If the objective is better policing, the money should go towards strengthening police stations, investigation, beat policing and manpower rather than creating multiple administrative establishments,” the former officer argued.
Public could face confusion
Another concern raised by the former DGP is the impact on the public. At present, Bengaluru residents broadly identify the city police commissioner as the head of the city police force. Under the proposed arrangement, there would be five commissioners functioning across different jurisdictions, in addition to a proposed Chief Police Commissioner. The former officer said this could create uncertainty among citizens about which commissionerate is responsible for a particular area or issue.
Instead of making policing more accessible, the arrangement could create confusion about jurisdiction, particularly when an incident involves more than one commissionerate, he said.
Former city commissioner favours leaner model
Another former city police commissioner also questioned the need for five independent commissionerates, while agreeing that Bengaluru needs greater decentralisation.
According to him, the city should ideally have no more than two commissionerates, with the rapidly expanding areas and rural belts beyond the Outer Ring Road brought under a separate commissionerate.
An ADGP-rank officer could head the new commissionerate, while existing Additional Superintendents of Police could be redesignated as DCPs and given greater territorial responsibility, he suggested.
Such a structure, he said, would provide decentralised policing without creating multiple layers of senior command.
Existing divisions had worked well
The former commissioner pointed to the restructuring undertaken in 2016, when new divisions such as Whitefield and Electronic City were created as Bengaluru expanded.
Several new police stations were established, while the Central Crime Branch was also given police-station powers. Despite resistance from some political leaders at the time, the restructuring subsequently helped the police manage the growing city, he said.
The creation of new divisions gave senior officers better control over their jurisdictions and reduced the burden on the central city police establishment.
The model was also relatively cost-effective and allowed the government to reorganise police jurisdictions as the city expanded, the former officer said.
Instead of creating five commissionerates, the existing system could be strengthened by adding more DCP-led divisions wherever population and policing requirements warrant it, he suggested.
Five commissionerates have supporters
The proposed restructuring, however, has its supporters among former police officials. Another former city police commissioner described the move as a positive step considering Bengaluru’s rapid growth and future expansion. The officer said dividing the city into five commissionerates could help address increasing demands relating to law and order, traffic management and local policing, provided there is effective coordination between the commissionerates.
Smaller jurisdictions could allow senior officers to devote greater attention to local problems and work more closely with the respective civic administrations, the officer said. The success of the system, however, would depend on clearly defining the jurisdiction, powers and responsibilities of each commissionerate and ensuring seamless coordination, the officer added.
Do five corporations need five commissionerates?
The larger debate centres on whether the five GBA corporations should automatically translate into five police jurisdictions.
Former officers opposing the model point out that organised crime, cybercrime, financial offences, drug networks and major law-and-order incidents frequently cross territorial boundaries. Major traffic corridors and public events can similarly affect several parts of the city.
They argue that police jurisdictions should instead be determined by population, crime patterns, geography, traffic movement, police-station workload and emergency response requirements, rather than simply mirroring civic boundaries.
While there is broad agreement that Bengaluru needs more police personnel, the additional manpower should strengthen police stations, investigation teams, beat policing, traffic enforcement, cybercrime investigation and specialised units.
Officers favouring a leaner structure argue that Bengaluru could achieve decentralisation through two or three strong commissionerates supported by expanded DCP divisions. Under such a model, the existing urban core could form one commissionerate, while the rapidly expanding peripheral and rural areas could come under another. Additional divisions could subsequently be created as the city grows.
The advantage, they argue, would be greater flexibility to reorganise police jurisdictions periodically without having to undertake a major restructuring of the entire city police establishment.
The larger question
The debate is not over whether Bengaluru needs police reform. There is broad agreement that the city’s expansion requires more manpower, stronger field-level supervision and better coordination.
The key question is whether these objectives are best achieved through five independent commissionerates or through a smaller number of stronger territorial units under a unified city police command. The former DGP said the government should carefully examine the operational consequences before implementing a system that could be difficult and expensive to reverse.
The success of any restructuring, retired officers said, should ultimately be measured not by the number of senior officers appointed or commissionerates created, but by whether it delivers faster response, effective force mobilisation, stronger investigations, better traffic management, clear accountability and improved policing at the police-station level. Whether these services can be delivered to the people is the bigger question.

briefs.headline: New line to strengthen power supply in Manyata-Hoodi areas in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: North and east Bengaluru — the wide arc which hosts Manyata Tech Park–Hoodi corridor — will soon get relief from frequent power outages with Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation (KPTCL) commissioning a 12-km-long 220 kV multi-circuit transmission line.
The stretch has witnessed a sharp increase in electricity consumption since the area has multinational companies, technology and business parks, large apartment complexes and rapidly expanding residential layouts. The additional capacity is expected to provide the grid with greater flexibility to handle further growth in electricity demand.
According to KPTCL officials, executing the project was a major engineering challenge since the corridor passes through a densely developed urban landscape, with limited space, busy roads, existing power lines and other infrastructure leaving little room for construction activity.
Ram Prasath Manohar, managing director of KPTCL, said the project demonstrated the importance of developing engineering solutions suited to Bengaluru’s constrained urban environment. KPTCL said the project was completed through planning, safety measures and coordination between multiple teams.
Energy minister KJ George said power demand in Bengaluru is continuously increasing, and the transmission infrastructure must be strengthened accordingly. “Every transmission project in an urban area requires a solution based on local conditions, technical feasibility and future system requirements. KPTCL has successfully addressed the challenges associated with this project,” he added.
KPTCL has commissioned a 12-km-long 220 kV multi-circuit transmission line to strengthen Bengaluru’s power grid and ease overloading and tripping along the high-demand Manyata Tech Park–Hoodi corridor.

briefs.headline: SIR: NDA defends bulk filing of Form 7, alleges ‘police intimidation’ by Congress; Karnataka CM hits back
briefs.bodyText:
Defending the filing of Form 7 applications (for objections and seeking deletions) in bulk, the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), comprising the BJP and JD(S), submitted a complaint to Governor Thaawarchand Gehlot on Tuesday, arguing that the Congress government was using the police machinery to intimidate BJP and JD(S) workers during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and that there was no bar on filing multiple Form 7 applications.
In their letter, the NDA said criminal cases were being registered against those filing Form 7 applications, with the Congress government creating “fear and apprehension” among objectors even when they were only exercising their “legitimate statutory right”.
The NDA cited an Election Commission of India statement dated January 16, 2026, and the Manual on Electoral Rolls, 2023 to argue that there was no restriction on the number of Form 7 applications that could be submitted to an ERO/AERO. It also pointed to provisions requiring objections to be cross-verified and said a Booth Level Agent (BLA) could file multiple Form 7 applications.
The alliance said the filing of an objection did not automatically result in the deletion of a name, as the ERO/AERO was required to follow the prescribed inquiry process.
The alliance alleged that the State government was using the police to intimidate objectors and that the cases were being filed under “political pressure”, specifically against BJP workers. It further alleged that even the CEO appeared to have “succumbed to the pressure”.
Biggest criminal conspiracy: CM
After the NDA alliance met the Karnataka CEO and the Governor, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar hit back on Tuesday, saying that the parties were plotting “a big criminal conspiracy in the history of India” and that, in many places, BJP workers had withdrawn their Form 7 applications and submitted written apologies.
“It is BJP workers who distributed Form 7. They must reveal who instructed them and supplied the pre-filled forms. Now they are trying to protect their workers. The workers will have to disclose who gave them the forms, and that has to be investigated,” he said here.
“In Babaleshwar, represented by Minister M.B. Patil, BJP leaders themselves have admitted that they distributed the forms, acknowledged it was wrong and requested that no action be taken. What do BJP leaders have to say about that?” Mr. Shivakumar asked, adding that the Congress was collecting documents related to the matter.
“It is the duty of anyone who feels that their vote has been snatched away to file a complaint, and hence we went to the CEO. Earlier, they (the BJP) were involved in the Chilume Trust case (the NGO accused of involvement in the alleged voter data theft controversy). I know the strategies of both the BJP and JD(S). It is my duty to protect voters, including their voters, for the sake of democracy.”

briefs.headline: Karnataka Dalit Entrepreneurs Association urges government to clear pending funds and land allotments
briefs.deck: According to the association, an industrial land subsidy of ₹825 crore meant for SC/ST entrepreneurs is currently pending from the government to the KIADB
briefs.bodyText:
Highlighting that the delay in the release of essential funds by the State government to the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB) has stalled new industrial projects for Scheduled Caste (SC) and Scheduled Tribe (ST) entrepreneurs, the Karnataka Dalit Entrepreneurs Association has called for the immediate release of the pending funds.
According to the association, an industrial land subsidy of ₹825 crore meant for SC/ST entrepreneurs is currently pending from the government to the KIADB. Due to the non-release of these funds, the process of approving new industrial projects for SC/ST entrepreneurs has been stalled.
“According to information gathered by the Association, about 33% of the total cases have various issues, such as disputed land, uneven plots, lack of basic amenities, and non-payment of compensation to landowners. Excluding these disputed cases, the Association estimates that the pending grant to be paid to KIADB is only about ₹510 crore,” a statement from the association said, demanding the immediate release of the amount.
The association also called for the disputed cases to be resolved quickly.
Prioritise pending allotments
Highlighting reservation backlogs, the statement further noted that the allotment of 391 acres of land under the SC/ST reservation quota remains pending, as per KIADB records and documents, and that the decision to rectify this shortfall was never implemented. The association also objected to the non-implementation of the KIADB Board’s 2014 decision to provide reservation for SC/ST entrepreneurs in old industrial areas developed before 2009.
“Several SC/ST entrepreneurs have obtained approval for their projects and have paid advance money years ago while waiting for industrial plot allotments. It is unjust that KIADB has issued new notifications for plot allotments without resolving these older pending cases. Priority must be given to settling these long-pending allotment cases of SC/ST entrepreneurs who paid advance deposits years ago before proceeding with any new allotment process,” the statement said.
“The Social Welfare Department, Scheduled Tribes Welfare Department, Department of Industries and Commerce, and Finance Department must work in coordination to resolve all pending issues related to SC/ST grants, reservations, land allotments and incentive schemes within a fixed time frame,” it added.

briefs.headline: Heavy rain leaves Bengaluru roads, underpasses waterlogged
briefs.deck: Traffic police officials said most instances of waterlogging were cleared overnight, shortly after they were reported, to ensure that the impact of the rain did not spill over into October 6 morning traffic
briefs.bodyText:
Heavy rains that lashed parts of Bengaluru since the afternoon of October 5 led to waterlogging in several parts of the city, slowing traffic on stretches including Laggere, Yeshwantpur and Hebbal, as well as in parts of south Bengaluru.
Traffic police officials said most instances of waterlogging were cleared overnight, shortly after they were reported, to ensure that the impact of the rain did not spill over into the morning traffic on October 6. However, in some areas, water remained stagnant due to the poor condition of roads, and efforts were under way to clear these stretches, officials said.
Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) officials said roads in Hennur, Doddanekundi, ITPL and Indiranagar, among other areas, were waterlogged. The Shivananda Circle and Hoodi underpasses were flooded. The officials added that there were only a few complaints of trees and branches falling, including in HAL and around Defence Colony, and these were attended to immediately.
Officials said work on stormwater drains had been carried out over the past few months to prevent flooding. As a result, no major instances of flooding were reported. Long-term measures to address flooding are also under way, they added.

stories.headline: Brent crosses $101 as Saudi attacks, US storm add to oil supply concerns
stories.deck: Rising oil prices, now exceeding 1%, raise alarms over potential storm disruptions affecting U.S. oil production and refineries. With Brent crude passing $101 per barrel and WTI crude hitting $90.38, concerns are amplified by supply issues from Saudi Arabia and mixed signals on U.S. inventories. Coupled with ongoing tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, analysts predict…
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices rose more than 1% on Wednesday, with Brent crude crossing the $101-a-barrel mark as fresh supply risks outweighed rising optimism due to increased Middle East crude supplies.
WTI crude rose 1.05% to $90.38 a barrel, while Brent crude gained 1.02% to $101.60 as supply concerns emerged in Saudi Arabia and the US oil and refining sector.
The latest concerns came from both sides of the global oil supply chain. According to US forecasters, a storm developing in the Gulf of Mexico is expected to become the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within two days and is likely to affect oil and gas facilities.
The areas in the storm's path account for 15% of US crude production and 5% of the country's natural gas production. Six refineries could also be affected. Refineries located in US Gulf states represent about 50% of the country's total refining capacity of 18.2 million barrels per day (bpd).
The prospect of disruption has emerged even as oil supplies from the Middle East have increased. Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman on Tuesday said that supply had been rising, with the East-West pipeline reaching 5.8 million barrels a day.
The head of Vitol said that around 12 million barrels per day of crude oil and 2 million bpd of refined products had been shipped out of the Middle East by tankers over the previous seven to 10 days.
US inventory data, however, offered a mixed picture. According to market sources citing by Reuters, crude and gasoline inventories declined last week, while distillate stocks increased marginally. US crude inventories fell by 2.09 million barrels in the week ended October 2.
Meanwhile, tensions around Saudi Arabia have added another risk to regional supply. The Saudi aviation authority said airports in Jazan and Najran were attacked twice on Monday evening as hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis escalated.
The attacks came as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pursued a major offensive to regain territory from the Houthis after weeks of rebel advances. Saudi Arabia has increased airstrikes in support of the campaign.
Mukesh Sahdev, chief oil analyst at X Analysts in Sydney, said the attacks and refinery outages could continue to support higher oil prices.
“Attacks and refinery outages are likely to keep the cracks elevated and scarcity will transmit to crude. Prices will stay elevated near a $100 level without any material de-escalation emerging,” Sahdev said.
The wider tensions involving Iran have also remained unresolved. US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that there was uncertainty over who was running Iran during the eight-month US-Israeli war with Iran.
"Their leaders are gone, their second group of leaders are gone, and the biggest problem I have is nobody knows who the hell is running the country," Trump said.
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said on Sunday that Washington knows very well who its counterpart is in Iran and how the decision-making system in the country works.

stories.headline: Why charging for UPI changes the math
stories.deck: If ₹100 collected in MDR causes more than ₹100 of economic value to disappear elsewhere, the payment system ends up better funded and the country poorer
stories.bodyText:
In the decade since its launch, India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has evolved from a promising digital experiment into critical economic infrastructure. Against this backdrop, the Union Finance Ministry has notified that the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) will operationalise a 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on specified merchant transactions above ₹2,000 from October 15. While consumers will not be charged directly, this marks a significant departure from UPI’s zero-MDR model for merchants. While the reasoning is understandable, considering the costs to run UPI, one question deserves an answer: what has UPI cost India, and what has it saved?
The costs are easy to see as servers, security and fraud controls show up on balance sheets, while the savings are scattered across the economy. For example, take a small shopkeeper. Before digital payments, taking cash meant counting notes, keeping change, guarding the till and making trips to the bank, with the added risk of theft. UPI removed most of that, with customers also saving themselves a few trips to the ATM. Further, banks now handle less physical cash, businesses reconcile accounts faster, lenders are able to read a small trader’s cash flow from digital records, and most importantly, the government gets a trail that helps with formalisation and tax compliance. None of this is revenue to UPI; it is spread across banks, consumers and the exchequer.

stories.headline: Women are twice as likely to use public transport for work commute | Data
stories.deck: Nearly 67% of all women who commuted to work relied on walking or buses or other public transport
stories.bodyText:
The National Household Travel Survey (NHTS), which captures how people in India travel to the workplace, shows a clear gender divide in mobility and the modes used to travel to work.
Data shows that women are twice as likely as men to commute to work using public transport such as buses or trains or on foot compared to men.
Nearly 67% of all women who commuted to work relied on walking or buses or other public transport. This figure was only 33% for all men who commuted to work.
In rural areas, more than half of all women who were working walked to their workplaces. However, a large share of men were dependent on two-wheelers.
While two-wheelers remained a major mode of transport for both men and women in urban areas, women were not solely reliant on two-wheelers.
A Statewise analysis shows that the share of women walking to work rather than relying on buses was higher than the national average in the central and northeastern States, including M.P., U.P. and Bihar
In States like M.P, U.P., Bihar and Chhattisgarh, rural women are overwhelmingly dependent on walking. For instance, in Madhya Pradesh, 88.7% of rural women walked and only 2.0% used the bus. This could signal either limited access to public transport or workplaces being far away.
In Keralam, only 20.1% of rural women walked, while 48.6% used the bus. This is the highest bus usage share among rural women in the country. In general, the share of women walking to work reduces in urban areas
While women in urban areas also rely on other means such as autos and cars, they still take slightly longer than men to commute to work. In at least 13 major States, a higher share of men commuted to work in around 30 minutes compared to women. As the survey doesn’t provide details on ownership, a granular analysis is not possible.
The use of public transport reflects the cost of commuting too. Though women’s expenditure on commute is lower than that of men in rural areas, the gap is reducing in urban areas.
The data for the charts were sourced from the National Household Travel Survey conducted by the National Statistics Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI). The survey was conducted between July 2025 and June 2026, covering 2,84,769 rural and 2,07,254 urban households. The analysis pertains only to the share of workers aged 15 and above, and a trip is defined as travel covering a distance of more than 1 km.
